title: Web performance
blurb: Core Web Vitals, loading, images, JavaScript cost and measuring what users actually feel, rather than guessing.

questions.q: What does Largest Contentful Paint (LCP) measure?
choices: When the browser receives the first byte of the HTML document
When every image, font and script on the page has finished loading
When the largest image or text block in the viewport is rendered
When the first pixel of any text or image is painted on screen
questions.why: LCP marks the render time of the largest image or text block visible in the viewport, a proxy for "the main content is there". The first byte is TTFB, the first paint of anything is FCP, and "everything loaded" is the `load` event, which users do not perceive directly.
questions.asked: A screening question; the follow-up is usually "what is the LCP element on your app's home page, and what delays it?"

questions.q: Which metric replaced First Input Delay (FID) as a Core Web Vital in March 2024?
choices: INP, which reports roughly the slowest interaction across the whole visit
TBT, which sums the blocking time of long tasks while the page loads
TTI, which marks when the main thread first stays idle for five seconds
FCP, which records when the first text or image is painted on screen
questions.why: Interaction to Next Paint became a Core Web Vital in March 2024. FID only timed the input delay of the first interaction; INP covers delay, handler time and the next paint for every click, tap and key press, and reports close to the worst one. TBT is a lab proxy for it, not a Core Web Vital.
questions.asked: Checks whether your performance knowledge is current; candidates still quoting FID have not looked since 2023.

questions.q: What are the "good" Core Web Vitals thresholds, assessed at the 75th percentile of page visits?
choices: LCP within 4 s, INP within 500 ms, CLS at most 0.25
LCP within 1 s, INP within 100 ms, CLS at most 0.05
LCP within 2.5 s, INP within 100 ms, CLS at zero
LCP within 2.5 s, INP within 200 ms, CLS at most 0.1
questions.why: Good is LCP at most 2.5 s, INP at most 200 ms and CLS at most 0.1, and a page passes when 75% of visits meet each one. The 4 s / 500 ms / 0.25 figures are the boundaries of "poor"; 100 ms was the old FID threshold.
questions.asked: Knowing the numbers and the 75th percentile shows you have read a real report rather than just heard the acronyms.

questions.q: Which of these layout shifts is excluded from Cumulative Layout Shift (CLS)?
choices: Text reflowing when a web font swaps in after the fallback font painted
Content moving within 500 ms of a click that expands an accordion panel
Content pushed down when an ad slot fills three seconds after load
Text pushed down when a hero image without dimensions finishes loading
questions.why: Shifts within 500 ms of a discrete user input (click, tap, key press) are flagged `hadRecentInput` and left out, because the user expects the page to change. The font swap, the late ad and the undimensioned image all move content the user did not ask to move, so they all count.
questions.asked: Separates people who know CLS is about unexpected movement from those who think any animation or expansion is penalised.

questions.q: Why can a standard Lighthouse page-load run NOT report INP?
choices: Lighthouse throttles the CPU, which makes interaction timings unreliable
INP is only collected on Android Chrome, not in desktop browsers
INP needs real interactions, and a page-load run never clicks or types
INP is taken from CrUX, which Lighthouse cannot query while offline
questions.why: INP is measured from user input, and a navigation audit only loads the page. Lab tools substitute Total Blocking Time as a proxy, or you script interactions with a timespan run. Throttling makes timings pessimistic, not impossible, and INP is measured by the browser itself, not fetched from CrUX.
questions.asked: Tests whether you understand why field data exists at all, which is the root of most "Lighthouse is green but users complain" confusion.

questions.q: Why does a `<link rel="stylesheet">` in the `<head>` delay the first paint?
choices: The browser will not render until the CSSOM is built, to avoid unstyled content
The HTML parser stops reading the document until the stylesheet has downloaded
The browser requests stylesheets one at a time before any images are requested
The CSS has to be parsed on the main thread after all scripts have finished
questions.why: CSS is render-blocking: layout needs the CSSOM, so nothing paints until the stylesheets in the head arrive and parse. It is not parser-blocking; the preload scanner keeps discovering images and scripts meanwhile. That is why critical CSS is inlined and non-critical CSS is loaded later.
questions.asked: The critical rendering path in one question; a strong answer mentions the render-blocking versus parser-blocking distinction.

questions.q: Your web font is referenced only from a stylesheet, so it is discovered late. Which resource hint fixes that?
choices: `prefetch`, which fetches the file early for the current page at high priority
`preconnect`, which downloads the font as soon as the head has been parsed
`dns-prefetch`, which resolves and then downloads the font file in the background
`preload` with `as="font"`, which fetches a file the current page needs, early
questions.why: `preload` fetches a resource this page will need before the parser would find it; fonts also need `crossorigin`. `prefetch` is a low-priority fetch for a likely next navigation, and `preconnect` / `dns-prefetch` only warm up the connection or DNS lookup without downloading anything.
questions.asked: Candidates often use the three hints interchangeably; the interviewer wants the "this page vs next page vs connection only" split.

questions.q: What does `font-display: swap` do here?
choices: Hides text for up to three seconds, then shows the fallback font
Shows fallback text at once, then swaps in Brand when it loads
Uses Brand only if it is cached already, else keeps the fallback
Downloads Brand at higher priority than the rest of the stylesheet
questions.why: `swap` gives an almost zero block period, so text is readable immediately in the fallback and is re-rendered when the font arrives. Hiding text for about three seconds is the `block`/`auto` behaviour, and "use it only if already available" describes `optional`. The trade-off of `swap` is a possible layout shift when the metrics differ.
questions.asked: Invisible text during font load is a common real bug; the follow-up is how to reduce the shift with `size-adjust` or a metric-matched fallback.

questions.q: This is the hero image at the top of the page. What does `loading="lazy"` do to LCP?
choices: Delays it, because the fetch waits until layout shows the image is in view
Nothing, because browsers ignore `lazy` on images in the initial viewport
Improves it, because lazy frees bandwidth for the hero image to load sooner
Removes it, because lazily loaded images are not eligible as LCP elements
questions.why: A lazy image cannot be fetched by the preload scanner; the browser waits until layout confirms it is near the viewport, so the LCP image starts downloading late. Browsers do not ignore the attribute above the fold; they honour it, just later than you would like. Use `lazy` only for below-the-fold images.
questions.asked: A frequent self-inflicted LCP regression when someone adds `lazy` to every `` in a component library.

questions.q: Why add `fetchpriority="high"` to the page's LCP image?
choices: It makes the browser decode the image off the main thread before paint
It tells the CDN edge to send this file ahead of other queued responses
Images start at low priority; this lets it compete with CSS and scripts
It forces the image to load even when the user has Data Saver turned on
questions.why: Browsers fetch images at low (or at best medium) priority until layout proves they are visible, so the hero can queue behind scripts. `fetchpriority="high"` raises it from the start. Off-thread decoding is what `decoding="async"` hints at, and the attribute says nothing to the CDN, which only sees an ordinary request.
questions.asked: Shows you know the browser's own priority rules, not just that "hints make things faster".

questions.q: A browser supports WebP but not AVIF. What does it download for this markup?
choices: `hero.avif` first, then `hero.webp` after the AVIF decode fails
`hero.jpg`, because the `img` src is always fetched as the fallback
`hero.webp` and `hero.jpg` together, then paints whichever lands first
Only `hero.webp`, the first source whose type it supports
questions.why: The browser walks the `source` elements in order and uses the first whose `type` it supports, so the AVIF is never requested and the JPEG is only a fallback for browsers that match nothing. AVIF and WebP usually give the same visual quality as JPEG in far fewer bytes, which is why the list starts with them.
questions.asked: Checks that you can ship modern formats without breaking older browsers or paying for two downloads.

questions.q: Your server compresses every response with brotli. Where does that actually save bytes?
choices: Mostly on JPEG and PNG, since images are the largest files on a page
On text such as HTML, CSS, JS and JSON; JPEG and AVIF are compressed already
Only on JavaScript, since browsers decompress no other content type
Only on responses over 1 MB; smaller ones cost more to decompress
questions.why: Brotli and gzip exploit repetition in text, so minified JS and CSS typically shrink by 70% or more, with brotli usually beating gzip by another 15-20%. Image and video formats are already compressed, so recompressing them wastes CPU for almost no gain. Browsers decompress any `Content-Encoding`, whatever the type.
questions.asked: A quick check that you know what compression is for, and a lead into "why is our image not getting smaller?".

questions.q: Your build emits `app.3f9a1c.js`. Why serve it with `Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable`?
choices: The hash changes whenever the content does, so this URL can be reused for a year unchecked
The browser re-downloads the file only when the ETag the server sends for it has changed
`immutable` stops CDNs and proxies from recompressing or altering the file while in transit
It lets the service worker refresh the file in the background on every visit to the site
questions.why: A content hash in the name means a new version gets a new URL, so the old URL can be cached for a year and `immutable` tells the browser not to revalidate it even on reload. ETags are for revalidation, which `immutable` skips, and "do not alter in transit" is `no-transform`. The HTML that references the file must NOT be cached like this.
questions.asked: The interviewer usually follows up with "so how do users get the new version?", which tests whether you know the HTML stays short-lived.

questions.q: Why is 300 KB of JavaScript more costly to a phone than a 300 KB JPEG?
choices: Scripts cannot be compressed, so they always travel at their full size
Scripts are never cached, so the bytes are paid again on every visit
The script must also be parsed, compiled and run on the main thread
Browsers download scripts one at a time but download images in parallel
questions.why: An image mostly decodes off the main thread, but every byte of script is parsed, compiled and executed on it, which on a mid-range phone can take several times longer than on a laptop. Scripts compress well and cache normally, so the transfer size is not the problem; the CPU cost is.
questions.asked: The core argument for shipping less JavaScript; a strong answer mentions testing on a mid-range device, not a MacBook.

questions.q: The project's package.json sets `"sideEffects": false`. After a production build, the polyfill never runs. Why?
choices: Bare imports with no binding are hoisted and only run after `start()` returns
Production builds only run polyfills in browsers that report missing features
Minifiers strip files that only modify globals such as `Array.prototype`
The bundler was told no module has side effects, so it dropped the bare import
questions.why: `sideEffects: false` promises the bundler that importing a module does nothing beyond its exports, so a bare import whose exports are unused is tree-shaken away. List the exceptions instead, for example `["./src/polyfills.js", "*.css"]`. Imports are not deferred: they are evaluated in order before `start()` runs.
questions.asked: A real production bug (also common with CSS imports) that shows whether you know what the flag promises, not just that it "enables tree shaking".

questions.q: Marketing adds six third-party tags through a tag manager, all loaded `async`. What is the most likely cost to users?
choices: Only load time grows; once loaded, third-party code runs on its own thread
Their scripts compete for the main thread, so interactions and INP get worse
Nothing measurable, since each third-party origin has its own connection pool
Only the first visit, since later ones reuse a cross-site cache of those files
questions.why: `async` only stops the download from blocking the parser; the code still runs on your main thread, adding long tasks and listeners that slow every interaction. Browsers have partitioned the HTTP cache by top-level site since about 2020, so a shared cross-site cache of popular scripts no longer exists.
questions.asked: Third-party scripts are often the biggest real-world cost, and the interviewer wants to hear that you would measure them and push back with data.

questions.q: Your main bundle grew from 180 KB to 420 KB in one release. What is the most direct way to find which dependency caused it?
choices: Run a bundle analyser treemap over the build and see which modules grew
Read the Lighthouse unused-JavaScript audit, which lists every package
Turn on production minification, which strips out code that was just added
Compare the gzip and brotli sizes to find the part that does not compress
questions.why: A bundle analyser (from source maps or the bundler's stats) shows each module's share of the output and who imports it, so a newly pulled-in date or icon library stands out at once. Lighthouse reports unused bytes per script file, not per package, and minification shrinks code without removing whole dependencies.
questions.asked: A practical question; the follow-up is usually how you would stop the regression happening again, which leads to budgets in CI.

questions.q: A click handler rebuilds a 5,000-row table and INP is 900 ms. Which line at the marked spot lets the browser paint the spinner first?
choices: `await Promise.resolve();` so the rebuild continues asynchronously
`await new Promise(queueMicrotask);` so the rebuild waits a microtask
`await scheduler.yield();` so the task ends and the browser can paint
No line: an `async` listener already lets the browser paint before it
questions.why: The next paint cannot happen until the current task ends. scheduler.yield() (Chrome 129+, Firefox 142+, not Safari, so feature-detect and fall back to await new Promise(r => setTimeout(r, 0))) ends the task and resumes the rest with priority, so the spinner paints first. Awaiting a resolved promise or a microtask resumes before rendering, so the page stays frozen for the whole rebuild; async alone changes nothing.
questions.asked: Shows whether you understand the event loop well enough to fix INP, rather than sprinkling `async` and hoping.

questions.q: Why does this image make the text below it jump?
questions.code: Free delivery on all orders this week.
choices: It lacks `loading="lazy"`, so it loads before the text next to it
JPEGs decode progressively, and each pass changes their height
Without `decoding="async"`, the image paint moves the other text
It has no `width` and `height`, so no space is reserved for it
questions.why: With no dimensions the browser lays the image out at zero height, then pushes everything down when the file arrives. `width` and `height` give it an aspect ratio to reserve space even under responsive CSS. The same fix applies to late-injected banners and ad slots: reserve their space up front.
questions.asked: The most common CLS cause; interviewers expect the one-line fix and a mention of reserving space for injected content.

questions.q: Lighthouse gives the page an LCP of 1.6 s, but CrUX reports 3.8 s at the 75th percentile. Which reflects users, and why?
choices: Lighthouse, because CrUX includes crawler traffic that drags the percentile up
CrUX, because it aggregates real devices and networks, not one simulated run
Lighthouse, because CrUX is a 28-day window that lags behind the latest deploy
Neither, because the gap means the LCP element differs from one run to the next
questions.why: CrUX is field data from real Chrome users on their own phones, networks and cache states; Lighthouse is a single lab run with fixed throttling. The 28-day window does lag a deploy, but it is still what users felt. Use lab tools to debug and field data to decide.
questions.asked: The lab-versus-field gap is where most performance arguments at work start, so interviewers want you to know which number to trust.

questions.q: In the Chrome DevTools Performance panel, a click shows a 400 ms interaction. Where do you look to find the cause?
choices: The main-thread flame chart under that interaction, to see which functions ran
The Network waterfall, to find the request the click was waiting on to finish
The Lighthouse report, which names the slowest event handler on the page
A Memory panel heap snapshot, to see how much the click handler allocated
questions.why: The interaction track shows input delay, processing and presentation; the main-thread flame chart below it shows exactly which handlers, renders or layouts filled that time. A network request does not block the next paint unless the handler waits synchronously, and Lighthouse does not attribute time to individual handlers.
questions.asked: Separates people who have actually profiled a slow interaction from those who only run Lighthouse.

questions.q: You add a performance budget to CI. Which set-up catches regressions without failing builds on noise?
choices: Fail the build whenever the Lighthouse performance score drops by a point
Fail on the field INP from CrUX, so the budget reflects real users directly
Gate on bundle bytes, and check lab timings as medians of several runs
Run Lighthouse once per pull request and fail on any increase in LCP
questions.why: Byte sizes are deterministic, so they make a reliable hard gate; lab timings vary run to run on shared CI machines, so take the median of several runs and set thresholds with headroom. CrUX is a 28-day aggregate of production traffic, so it cannot judge a pull request that has not shipped.
questions.asked: A budget that flakes gets switched off within a month; interviewers want to hear how you would make one that the team keeps.

questions.q: Your hashed JS and CSS are cached for a year. Which header should `index.html` get so users see a new deploy on their next visit without refetching it on every navigation?
choices: Cache-Control: no-store, so the browser never keeps a copy and always downloads fresh HTML in full
Cache-Control: max-age=31536000, immutable, matching the assets it references
Cache-Control: no-cache plus an ETag, so each visit revalidates and gets a 304 if unchanged
No Cache-Control at all, since browsers never cache HTML documents
questions.why: `no-cache` means 'store it, but revalidate before use': with an ETag or Last-Modified the browser sends a conditional request and gets a cheap 304 until you deploy, at which point the new HTML points at new hashed file names. `no-store` forces a full download every time and disables back/forward restore; a year-long `max-age` on the HTML would pin users to the old asset names. Browsers do cache HTML heuristically when no header is sent, which is the worst of both.
questions.asked: It is the second half of the immutable-assets pattern, and confusing `no-cache` with `no-store` is one of the most common HTTP caching mistakes.

questions.q: LCP is often broken into four sub-parts. Which list is correct, in order?
choices: DNS lookup, TCP connect, TLS handshake, and first byte of the HTML
TTFB, resource load delay, resource load duration, element render delay
First paint, first contentful paint, speed index, and time to interactive
Parse HTML, build CSSOM, run JavaScript, and composite the final layers
questions.why: TTFB is time to the first byte of HTML; load delay is the gap before the LCP resource starts downloading; load duration is its download; render delay is the gap until it paints. Breaking LCP down tells you whether to fix the server, discovery, bytes or main-thread blocking. The first option is all inside TTFB.
questions.asked: The sub-part breakdown turns "LCP is slow" into a specific fix, which is what interviewers want to hear.

questions.q: The LCP element is a hero image set with `background-image` in a stylesheet. Why is its resource load delay large?
questions.code: .hero { background-image: url(/img/hero.avif); }
choices: Background images are always decoded on the main thread, unlike ``
Background images never count as LCP candidates, so LCP falls back late
The preload scanner cannot see CSS images; they wait for CSS and style
Browsers download CSS images at the lowest priority after every script
questions.why: The preload scanner finds `` in the HTML immediately, but a CSS background is only requested after the stylesheet downloads and a matching element gets styled. Use an `` (with `fetchpriority="high"`) or preload it. CSS background images can be LCP candidates.
questions.asked: Tests understanding of resource discovery, the most overlooked part of LCP.

questions.q: A client-rendered React SPA has a slow LCP even though the hero image is small and cached on a CDN. What is the most likely cause?
choices: The image does not exist until the JS bundle loads, runs and renders
CDNs serve images with lower priority to SPAs than to server-rendered pages
LCP always includes JavaScript parse time, whatever the page's element is
React replaces `` with canvas drawing, which paints only after idle
questions.why: With client-side rendering the HTML is an empty shell, so the `` does not exist until the bundle has loaded and rendered, pushing resource load delay and render delay up. Server rendering or static HTML for the shell, or preloading the image, puts it back on the fast path.
questions.asked: Connects rendering strategy to Web Vitals, a common SSR-vs-CSR discussion point.

questions.q: Which `` lets the preload scanner fetch a responsive LCP image early, choosing the same candidate as the `` will?
choices: `<link rel="prefetch" href="/hero-800.avif">` for the middle size
`<link rel="preload" as="image" imagesrcset imagesizes>`
`<link rel="preconnect" href="/img/hero.avif" as="image">` early on
`<link rel="modulepreload" href="/img/hero.avif">` in the head
questions.why: `imagesrcset` and `imagesizes` mirror `srcset` and `sizes`, so the preload picks the same file the `` will use and nothing is downloaded twice. `prefetch` is low priority for future navigations, `preconnect` takes an origin not a file, and `modulepreload` is for JS modules.
questions.asked: Preloading one fixed size of a responsive image wastes bytes; interviewers like candidates who know this variant.

questions.q: INP is made up of three phases for each interaction. Which list is right?
choices: Input delay, processing duration, and presentation delay
Network time, parse time, and time to first byte of data
Hover delay, focus delay, and the paint of the next frame
Script evaluation, garbage collection, and GPU compositing
questions.why: Input delay is waiting for the main thread to be free; processing is running your event handlers; presentation delay is the style, layout and paint work before the next frame. Long tasks cause the first, heavy handlers the second, and large DOM updates the third.
questions.asked: Knowing the phases lets you say which fix targets which part, which is the real interview test.

questions.q: Which of these user actions is NOT measured by INP?
choices: Clicking a "Save" button with the mouse
Tapping a checkbox on a phone touchscreen
Pressing Enter in a search field to submit it
Scrolling the page with the mouse wheel
questions.why: INP observes clicks, taps and key presses. Scrolling and hovering are not interactions for INP, because they are usually handled off the main thread by the compositor. A janky scroll is still bad, but it will not show up in INP.
questions.asked: A quick check that you know what the metric actually observes.

questions.q: A visit has 120 interactions. Roughly which one does INP report?
choices: The very first interaction, as First Input Delay did before it
The mean of all 120 interaction latencies over the whole visit
Near the worst, ignoring one outlier per 50 interactions
The median interaction latency, to smooth out one-off slow events
questions.why: INP takes the longest interaction, but on pages with many interactions it discards one outlier for every 50, so here it reports about the third longest. That keeps one freak event from dominating while still reflecting the slow tail. FID looked only at the first input's delay.
questions.asked: A detail that shows you have read how the metric is computed rather than just its threshold.

questions.q: A search field filters 2,000 rows on every keystroke and INP is poor. Which change reduces processing duration most directly?
choices: Move the listener from `input` to `keyup`, which fires less often
Wrap `renderRows` in `requestAnimationFrame` to run it after paint
Change the handler to `async`, so that the filtering runs in parallel
Update the input at once and debounce the filter and render work
questions.why: The field already shows the typed character natively; debouncing the expensive filter and render means most keystrokes do little work and the next frame paints quickly. `async` does not create parallelism, `keyup` fires just as often, and `requestAnimationFrame` runs before the next paint, not after it.
questions.asked: The canonical INP fix; the rAF distractor catches people who think it means "later".

questions.q: Which API shows you which scripts caused slow frames in the field, with attribution to source URLs and functions?
choices: The Long Animation Frames API (`long-animation-frame` entries)
The Navigation Timing API (`navigation` entries in the buffer)
The Resource Timing API (`resource` entries for each download)
The Paint Timing API (`first-contentful-paint` entry only)
questions.why: LoAF (Chrome 123+) reports frames longer than 50 ms with script attribution such as `sourceURL`, `invoker` and duration, so field INP data can be tied to a specific script. The older Long Tasks API had almost no attribution. The web-vitals attribution build uses LoAF.
questions.asked: Field attribution is how teams actually fix INP at scale; knowing LoAF marks recent hands-on work.

questions.q: Why can a page with a huge DOM (say 15,000 nodes) have a poor INP even when its event handlers are fast?
choices: Large DOMs stop the browser from dispatching events to handlers
Style recalculation and layout after each update take a long time
INP counts every node the handler reads as a separate interaction
Garbage collection runs before each click on pages above 10,000 nodes
questions.why: After handlers run, the browser must recalculate styles and lay out affected nodes before it can paint, and that cost scales with DOM size, showing up as presentation delay. Virtualising long lists or `content-visibility: auto` for off-screen sections reduces it.
questions.asked: Moves the conversation past "make the handler faster" to rendering cost, which strong candidates raise unprompted.

questions.q: What does `content-visibility: auto` on long, below-the-fold sections do?
choices: Hides the sections from screen readers until they are scrolled into view
Lazy-loads the sections' HTML from the server when they approach the view
Lets the browser skip layout and paint for sections until they near view
Moves the sections to a separate GPU layer so scrolling them is smoother
questions.why: Off-screen sections with `content-visibility: auto` skip rendering work, which cuts initial rendering time and the cost of later updates. Pair it with `contain-intrinsic-size` so the scrollbar does not jump. Content stays in the DOM and accessibility tree, and nothing is fetched.
questions.asked: A modern CSS lever for rendering cost; mentioning `contain-intrinsic-size` shows you have used it.

questions.q: How does CLS group layout shifts into a single score for a page visit?
choices: It sums every layout shift from load until the page is finally unloaded
It takes the worst window of shifts (under 1 s apart, 5 s at most)
It records the single largest shift that happens during the whole visit
It averages all shifts that occur within the first five seconds of load
questions.why: Shifts are grouped into session windows (a window ends after a 1 s gap or at 5 s long), and CLS is the largest window's total. That stopped long-lived SPAs from accumulating ever-growing scores. It still covers the whole visit, not just loading.
questions.asked: Explains why CLS can be bad on a page that loads cleanly, if something shifts later.

questions.q: An expanding panel animates its `height` and pushes content below. A toast slides in using `transform: translateY()`. Which one can produce layout shifts?
choices: The toast, since any `transform` counts as moving the element's layout
Neither, because animations are always excluded from CLS measurement
The height animation, if it runs without recent input from the user
Each of them, since each one changes what is painted on the screen
questions.why: Layout-affecting properties like `height`, `top` and `margin` move other elements, which counts as a shift unless it follows user input within 500 ms. `transform` moves pixels without changing layout, so it is never a layout shift and is also cheaper to animate.
questions.asked: Tests whether you know why "animate transform and opacity" is standard advice.

questions.q: A web font loads late and the text reflows because the fallback font is wider. Which CSS reduces that shift without hiding text?
choices: `font-display: block;` so text stays invisible until the web font arrives
`size-adjust` with `ascent-override` so the fallback matches the metrics
`unicode-range: U+0000-00FF;` so only Latin glyphs are ever downloaded
`font-weight: 100 900;` so that the fallback covers every weight used
questions.why: Metric overrides (`size-adjust`, `ascent-override`, `descent-override`, `line-gap-override`) make a local fallback occupy nearly the same space as the web font, so the swap barely moves anything. Frameworks such as Next.js generate these automatically. `block` hides text and still shifts when it swaps.
questions.asked: The modern fix for font CLS; interviewers who have fought it will recognise the term.

questions.q: A cookie consent banner is inserted at the top of `<body>` after load and pushes the page down. What is the CLS-friendly alternative?
choices: Insert it after a `setTimeout` of five seconds so the shift is ignored
Insert it just above the footer so the shift happens below the viewport
Overlay it with `position: fixed`, or reserve its space up front
Insert it with `opacity: 0`, then fade it in so the move is not counted
questions.why: A fixed-position overlay does not move other content, and space reserved in the initial HTML means nothing shifts when it appears. Delaying the insert still shifts, and an invisible element that takes space shifts content when it is inserted, not when it becomes visible.
questions.asked: Banners and ads are real CLS sources; interviewers expect "reserve space or overlay".

questions.q: A page is restored from the back/forward cache (bfcache). What happens to its Core Web Vitals in the field?
choices: The visit is discarded from CrUX, since no network requests were made
It counts as a new page view with near-instant LCP, helping p75
It reuses the metrics from the original visit without any new entry
It counts as a failed page load, because `load` does not fire again
questions.why: bfcache restores are treated as separate page views (the web-vitals library reports them via `pageshow` with `persisted`), with LCP and CLS near zero, so enabling bfcache improves field numbers. Avoid `unload` listeners, which make pages ineligible.
questions.asked: bfcache eligibility is a cheap field win that many teams miss; knowing `unload` blocks it is the key detail.

questions.q: Which of these makes a page ineligible for the back/forward cache in Chrome?
choices: Registering a `pagehide` listener that saves a draft to storage
Registering an `unload` event listener anywhere on the page
Serving the HTML with `Cache-Control: max-age=0` and an ETag
Loading scripts with `type="module"` rather than classic scripts
questions.why: `unload` listeners block bfcache in Chrome and are being deprecated. `pagehide` and `visibilitychange` are the reliable replacements and are bfcache-friendly. Normal revalidation headers and module scripts do not matter; open connections such as WebSockets can also block it.
questions.asked: A practical one; DevTools' Application panel has a bfcache test that lists exactly these blockers.

questions.q: TTFB for your HTML is 1.8 s at p75. Why does fixing it matter for LCP?
choices: It does not; TTFB is a network metric, and LCP only measures rendering
Every LCP sub-part starts after TTFB, so it sets a floor for LCP
LCP subtracts TTFB, so a slow server makes LCP look better than it is
TTFB only affects INP, because the first interaction waits for HTML
questions.why: Nothing can be discovered or painted until the HTML starts arriving, so TTFB is the first slice of every LCP. At 1.8 s you have used most of the 2.5 s budget before the browser sees a single tag. Server caching, a CDN, fewer redirects or streaming the head early all help.
questions.asked: Checks that you look at the backend when LCP is slow rather than only at images.

questions.q: What does sending a `103 Early Hints` response do for a slow-to-render HTML page?
questions.code:
HTTP/1.1 103 Early Hints
Link: </css/app.css>; rel=preload; as=style

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: text/html
choices: The browser can fetch critical assets while the server builds the HTML
It tells the browser the HTML is cached, so the 200 response can be skipped
It downgrades the connection to HTTP/1.1 so that preloads can be multiplexed
It pushes the stylesheet body inside the 103 response, like HTTP/2 Server Push
questions.why: A 103 is an interim response carrying `Link` headers, so the browser can preconnect or preload during server think-time before the 200 arrives. Unlike the retired HTTP/2 Server Push, it sends hints rather than bodies, so the browser's cache is respected. It needs CDN or server support.
questions.asked: A good answer contrasts it with Server Push and explains why hints beat pushed bytes.

questions.q: Which navigation hint lets Chrome fully render the likely next page in the background so it appears instantly on click?
questions.code:
<script type="speculationrules">
{ "prerender": [{ "where": { "href_matches": "/orders/*" },
                  "eagerness": "moderate" }] }
</script>
choices: The Speculation Rules API with `prerender`, as shown here
A `<link rel="preload">` for the next page's HTML document URL
A `<link rel="dns-prefetch">` for the origin of the next page
A service worker that caches `/orders/*` responses on install
questions.why: Speculation rules can prefetch or prerender same-site pages; `moderate` eagerness triggers on hover or pointer down. Prerendering runs the page, so avoid it for URLs with side effects and count analytics carefully. `preload` is for subresources of the current page, and a service worker cache still has to render on click.
questions.asked: A Chromium feature teams use for near-instant multi-page navigations; knowing the side-effect caveat matters.

questions.q: Your field data shows good LCP on desktop but poor LCP on mobile. Which fix is most likely to target the mobile gap?
choices: Adding more CPU cores to the server that renders the page HTML
Right-sized images via `srcset`, so phones download less
Minifying the HTML, which is usually most of a page's weight
Increasing the CDN cache TTL from one day to one full year
questions.why: Phones have slower networks and CPUs and often receive the same desktop-sized hero image. Responsive images cut bytes on the LCP resource directly. Server CPU would affect both device classes, HTML is rarely the heavy part, and TTL changes affect cache hit rates, not device differences.
questions.asked: Checks that you segment field data by device before choosing a fix.

questions.q: What is the "good" threshold for Time to First Byte recommended by web.dev?
choices: 0.8 seconds or less at the 75th percentile
2.5 seconds or less at the 75th percentile
200 milliseconds or less at the median
100 milliseconds or less for every request
questions.why: TTFB is not a Core Web Vital, but 0.8 s is the suggested good threshold because it leaves room for the rest of LCP within 2.5 s. 2.5 s is the LCP threshold and 200 ms the INP threshold, which is where the distractors come from.
questions.asked: Knowing thresholds by heart lets you read a PageSpeed report quickly in a pairing exercise.

questions.q: The LCP element is a paragraph in a web font with `font-display: block`, and the font loads slowly. What happens to LCP?
choices: It paints at once in the fallback font, and LCP records that paint time
It is hidden for up to about 3 s, and LCP waits for the visible text
It is excluded from LCP, since text in web fonts never counts as content
It paints in the web font from the HTTP cache on every visit, even cold
questions.why: `block` gives the font a short block period (about 3 s) during which text is invisible, so text-based LCP waits for the font or the timeout. `swap` or `optional` paint fallback text immediately. Text in web fonts is a normal LCP candidate.
questions.asked: Connects font loading to LCP, not just CLS, which many candidates miss.

questions.q: What is the difference between `defer` and `async` on a classic `<script src>` in the `<head>`?
choices: `defer` runs after parsing, in document order; `async` runs on arrival, in any order
`defer` downloads after parsing finishes; `async` downloads while the HTML parses
`defer` runs before `DOMContentLoaded` only in Chrome; `async` is the standard form
`defer` keeps blocking the parser while it runs; `async` never touches the main thread
questions.why: Both download in parallel with parsing. `defer` scripts execute after the document is parsed, in the order they appear, before `DOMContentLoaded`; `async` scripts execute as soon as each arrives, pausing the parser and in no guaranteed order. Neither delays the download itself.
questions.asked: A classic screening question; a strong answer says which one you'd use for app code (defer) and which for independent analytics (async).

questions.q: How does `<script type="module" src="/app.js">` behave by default with respect to parsing?
choices: It blocks the parser like a classic script until it has run
It runs as soon as it downloads, like a classic `async` script
It is deferred: fetched in parallel and run after parsing completes
It is fetched only when the page becomes idle after the `load` event
questions.why: Module scripts are deferred by default, so adding `defer` does nothing. Adding `async` makes them run as soon as they and their imports are ready. They never block the parser the way a plain classic script does.
questions.asked: Checks whether you know what Vite's default output does to the critical path without extra attributes.

questions.q: Your hero `` has `srcset` with 400w, 800w and 1600w files but no `sizes` attribute. What goes wrong on a phone where the image is 360 CSS px wide?
choices: The browser ignores `srcset` entirely and downloads the fallback `src` file instead
The browser assumes `100vw`, which here is close, so nothing goes wrong
The browser downloads all three files and keeps the best one for later
Without `sizes` the browser assumes `100vw`, which is only right if full-width
questions.why: With `w` descriptors and no `sizes`, the browser assumes the image is `100vw` wide. That is fine for a full-width hero but oversizes images shown in a narrow column; it never downloads every candidate. The trap is thinking `srcset` alone is enough for images in a grid or sidebar.
questions.asked: Responsive image markup is often copied without `sizes`; interviewers want you to know what the default does.

questions.q: Why should every `` have `width` and `height` attributes, even when CSS makes it responsive?
choices: They force the browser to download the image file at exactly 640 by 360 pixels
They give the browser an aspect ratio, so it reserves space before loading
They override the CSS, so the image never scales below 640 pixels wide
They let the browser skip decoding, as the dimensions are already known
questions.why: Modern browsers map the attributes to a default `aspect-ratio`, so with `height: auto` the box is sized correctly before a single byte arrives and nothing below it shifts. The attributes do not control which file is downloaded and CSS still wins for the rendered size.
questions.asked: The single most common CLS fix; interviewers expect it immediately after "what causes layout shift?".

questions.q: What does `decoding="async"` on an `` change?
choices: It downloads the image on a background thread instead of the main thread
It defers the download until the image scrolls near the viewport
It lets the browser present other content before this image is decoded
It switches the image to a progressive format the browser decodes faster
questions.why: `decoding` is a hint about whether the image's decode may be done off the critical path of presenting other content; it has nothing to do with when the download starts. Lazy downloading is `loading="lazy"`, and format is decided by the file itself.
questions.asked: A deeper image question; strong candidates add that the gain is small and that `loading` and `fetchpriority` matter far more.

questions.q: Which images on a long product listing page should get `loading="lazy"`?
choices: Every image on the page, including the first row, for the smallest payload
Only images inside ``, because a plain `` ignores the attribute
Only the LCP image, so that it does not compete with scripts for bandwidth
Images below the first screenful, but not those likely to be in the viewport
questions.why: Native lazy loading defers off-screen images until the user scrolls near them, saving bytes. Applied to images in the initial viewport it delays them (and often LCP) because the browser must lay out the page before it knows they are visible. It works on plain `` and `
questions.asked: Tests whether you apply lazy loading with judgement rather than as a blanket rule.

questions.q: A landing page auto-plays a 6 MB animated GIF. What is the usual performance fix?
choices: Convert it to a muted, looping MP4 or WebM `<video>` with a poster image
Convert it to an animated SVG, which the browser can rasterise on the GPU
Keep the GIF but add `loading="lazy"` so it downloads after the `load` event
Split it into frames and animate them with `setInterval` in JavaScript
questions.why: GIF is a very inefficient format for motion; the same clip as H.264 or AV1 video is often 5–20 times smaller and decodes in hardware. `autoplay muted loop playsinline` reproduces GIF behaviour. Lazy loading only moves the cost, and SVG is for vector drawings, not photographic frames.
questions.asked: A quick win question; interviewers like hearing the attribute list that makes a video behave like a GIF.

questions.q: Which is the right way to preload a self-hosted WOFF2 font used on the first screen?
choices: `<link rel="preload" href="/f/inter.woff2" as="font">` without other attributes
`<link rel="preload" href="/f/inter.woff2" as="font" type="font/woff2" crossorigin>`
`<link rel="prefetch" href="/f/inter.woff2" as="font" crossorigin>` in the head
`<link rel="preconnect" href="/f/inter.woff2" crossorigin>` before the CSS
questions.why: Fonts are always fetched in CORS mode, even same-origin, so a preload without `crossorigin` does not match the real request and the font downloads twice. `prefetch` is a low-priority hint for future navigations and `preconnect` takes an origin, not a file.
questions.asked: The missing `crossorigin` double download is a well-known bug; spotting it shows real DevTools experience.

questions.q: Your site ships a 400 KB font file covering Latin, Cyrillic and Greek, but serves only English content. What is the most effective fix?
choices: Add `font-display: optional`, which also stops the unused glyphs downloading
Convert the TTF to WOFF, since WOFF compresses glyph tables most tightly
Subset the font to the Latin range and declare it with `unicode-range`
Inline the whole font as base64 in the CSS to save the extra HTTP request
questions.why: Subsetting removes glyphs you never render, often cutting the file by 70–90%, and `unicode-range` lets the browser fetch other subsets only if those characters appear. `font-display` changes rendering, not bytes; WOFF2 (not WOFF) is the best compression; base64 inflates the size by about a third and blocks CSS.
questions.asked: Shows you look at what is inside an asset rather than only how it is delivered.

questions.q: What does `font-display: optional` trade off compared with `swap`?
choices: It shows fallback text at once and only uses the web font if it is ready almost immediately
It hides text for up to 3 s, then swaps to the web font whenever the file finally arrives
It loads the font only when the user opts in through the browser's font settings
It downloads the web font only on fast connections, which the browser detects
questions.why: `optional` has a tiny block period (about 100 ms) and no swap period: if the font is not ready, the fallback stays for that page view, so there is no late reflow. The font still downloads and is cached for the next view. `swap` always switches later, which can cause a layout shift.
questions.asked: Interviewers use it to see whether you can choose between brand fidelity and layout stability.

questions.q: What does `<link rel="preconnect" href="https://cdn.example.com" crossorigin>` do?
choices: It downloads the CDN's root document so later requests are served from cache
It opens DNS, TCP and TLS to that origin early, before any request needs it
It tells the CDN to push the page's assets over the current HTTP/2 connection
It resolves only the DNS name, leaving the TCP and TLS handshakes for later
questions.why: `preconnect` warms up a full connection (DNS, TCP and TLS) so the first real request saves one or more round trips; `dns-prefetch` does only the DNS part. Nothing is downloaded, and HTTP/2 server push has been removed from Chrome.
questions.asked: Checks you know the hint family: preconnect, dns-prefetch, preload, prefetch, and when each fits.

questions.q: A developer adds `preconnect` hints for eleven third-party origins "to be safe". What is the likely effect?
choices: No effect at all, because browsers ignore more than three preconnect hints
Faster loading overall, because every idle connection is effectively free
A CSP violation, because preconnect needs a matching `connect-src` entry
Wasted handshakes that compete with critical requests; most go unused
questions.why: Each preconnect costs CPU and bandwidth for the handshake and the connection is closed if not used within about 10 s. Preconnect to the one or two origins used in the critical path and use `dns-prefetch` for the rest. Browsers do not have a fixed cap of three.
questions.asked: Tests whether you treat hints as trade-offs rather than free speed.

questions.q: You preload six scripts, three fonts and four images in the `<head>`. Why might LCP get worse?
choices: Preloads are high priority, so too many compete with the LCP image for bandwidth
Preloaded resources are never cached, so the browser fetches each one twice
Browsers stop parsing the HTML until every preloaded resource has fully downloaded
Preloads run only after the `load` event, which pushes back the whole page
questions.why: Preload moves a resource to the front of the queue; if everything is preloaded, nothing is prioritised and the truly critical request waits behind the rest. Preloads do not block parsing and are cached normally, although an unused preload wastes bandwidth and triggers a console warning.
questions.asked: Overusing preload is a common regression; interviewers want to hear "preload only what is late-discovered and critical".

questions.q: What is "critical CSS" and why do teams inline it?
choices: The CSS for above-the-fold content, inlined so first paint need not wait for a stylesheet
The CSS rules that use `!important`, inlined so that no later stylesheet can override them
The CSS generated by a framework at build time, inlined to avoid a hydration mismatch
The CSS for error states, inlined so the page still renders if the CDN fails
questions.why: External stylesheets are render-blocking, so the first screen cannot paint until they download. Inlining the small set of rules needed for the first screen in a `<style>` tag lets it paint after the HTML alone, with the full stylesheet loaded without blocking. The cost is extra HTML bytes on every page and duplicated rules.
questions.asked: A follow-up to "why is CSS render-blocking?"; a strong answer mentions the cache trade-off.

questions.q: What does `media="print"` on this stylesheet link change about loading?
questions.code: <link rel="stylesheet" href="/print.css" media="print">
choices: The file is not downloaded at all unless the user actually prints the page
The file downloads at low priority and does not block rendering on screen
The file blocks rendering exactly as a normal stylesheet does on screen
The file is applied to the screen too, but only after the `load` event
questions.why: Browsers still download stylesheets whose media query does not match, but at low priority and without blocking first paint. That is why `media` is the correct way to split print or wide-screen styles, and why the old `media="print" onload` trick loads CSS asynchronously.
questions.asked: Shows you understand render-blocking as a per-media decision, not a property of every `<link>`.

questions.q: What is the purpose of splitting a React SPA's bundle by route with dynamic `import()`?
choices: It makes each component render faster, because smaller files parse quicker
It removes unused exports from each module, which static imports cannot do
It lets the browser cache the whole app for a year, whatever changes later
Users download only the code for the page they visit, plus shared chunks
questions.why: Dynamic `import()` creates a split point, so the bundler emits a separate chunk loaded on demand; the first page then needs far less JavaScript to download, parse and run. Removing unused exports is tree shaking, which works on static imports, and render speed per component does not change.
questions.asked: Code splitting is the first answer to "our bundle is too big"; interviewers then ask where you would split.

questions.q: In React 19 you wrap a route in `lazy()`. What must also be present so the app does not crash on first navigation?
questions.code:
const Reports = lazy(() => import('./Reports'));
// <Route path="/reports" element={<Reports />} />
choices: A `useEffect` that calls `import('./Reports')` again once the route mounts
A `<Suspense fallback>` boundary above it to show while the chunk loads
A `"use client"` directive at the top of `Reports.tsx` for the chunk to split
A `React.memo` around `Reports`, so the chunk loads only once per session
questions.why: A lazy component suspends while its chunk downloads, and React needs a `Suspense` boundary above it to show the fallback. `"use client"` is a Server Components directive, and `memo` has nothing to do with loading code.
questions.asked: Basic but practical; interviewers may follow up on where to place the boundary so the whole layout does not flash.

questions.q: Why does this import defeat tree shaking in a Vite or webpack production build?
questions.code:
import _ from 'lodash';
export const slug = (s: string) => _.kebabCase(s);
choices: Default imports are always stripped out in production builds by the minifier
TypeScript compiles `import` to `require`, which bundlers cannot analyse
`lodash` is CommonJS with one default object, so the whole library is kept
Tree shaking only removes code from your files, never from `node_modules`
questions.why: The `lodash` package is CommonJS and exposes a single object; the bundler cannot prove which properties are unused, so all of it ships. Use `lodash-es` with named imports or the per-method package. Tree shaking does work on ES module packages in `node_modules`.
questions.asked: A realistic bundle review question; the strong answer names the ESM alternative and how you would verify with a visualiser.

questions.q: Which change typically shrinks a production bundle that includes Moment.js with all its locales?
choices: Enable gzip on the dev server, which the bundle analyser measures
Switch to `Intl.DateTimeFormat` or a modular library such as date-fns
Mark `moment` as a `devDependency` so the bundler leaves it out
Add `"type": "module"` to package.json so Moment becomes tree-shakeable
questions.why: Moment is large, mutable and not tree-shakeable, and its locale files are pulled in wholesale. The built-in `Intl` APIs handle most formatting for zero bytes, and date-fns imports per function. Whether a package is a devDependency has no effect on what the bundler includes if you import it.
questions.asked: Interviewers want to hear that you check whether the platform already does the job before adding a dependency.

questions.q: What does a `browserslist` target of only modern browsers usually save in a Vite 7 build?
choices: Nothing measurable, because Vite always outputs ES5 for compatibility
Image bytes, because modern targets let Vite convert all images to AVIF
Server time, because modern browsers skip the TLS handshake on revisit
Transpilation and polyfills, so less JavaScript ships to every user
questions.why: When the target supports native syntax such as classes, async functions and optional chaining, the compiler does not down-level it and no polyfills are injected, so bundles are smaller and faster to parse. Vite's default target is already modern browsers; it does not emit ES5 unless you add the legacy plugin.
questions.asked: Shows you know build targets are a performance setting, not just a compatibility one.

questions.q: A long list view renders 10,000 rows and scrolling stutters. What is the standard fix?
choices: Virtualise the list so only the rows near the viewport exist in the DOM
Wrap each row in `React.memo` so none of them ever needs to render
Move the rows into an `<iframe>` so that they paint on a separate thread
Add `will-change: transform` to every row so the GPU draws them all
questions.why: Virtualisation (windowing) keeps the DOM small by rendering only visible rows plus a buffer, so style, layout and paint stay cheap. `memo` avoids re-renders but the 10,000 nodes still exist; `will-change` on thousands of elements creates thousands of layers and uses a lot of memory.
questions.asked: Common in CRUD admin apps; interviewers may ask about the accessibility and find-in-page cost of virtualising.

questions.q: Why is this loop slow?
choices: `style.width` must be set with `setProperty`, or it triggers a full repaint
Reading `offsetWidth` after each write forces a fresh synchronous layout
`for...of` over a NodeList copies every element into a new array first
String concatenation in a loop allocates enough to trigger garbage collection
questions.why: Each write invalidates layout and the next `offsetWidth` read forces the browser to recalculate it immediately; this is layout thrashing (forced synchronous layout). Read once before the loop, then do all the writes. `setProperty` and `style.width` behave the same.
questions.asked: The canonical forced-reflow question; DevTools flags it as "Forced reflow" and interviewers like hearing that.

questions.q: Which CSS properties can be animated without triggering layout or paint on each frame?
choices: `width` and `height`, because their values are already known to the layout engine
`top` and `left`, because absolutely positioned boxes skip the layout stage
`transform` and `opacity`, which the compositor can apply on its own
`margin` and `padding`, because they change spacing but not the content
questions.why: `transform` and `opacity` changes can be handled by the compositor on an existing layer, so the main thread does no layout or paint per frame. Animating `top`, `left`, `width` or `margin` triggers layout every frame, even for positioned elements.
questions.asked: Interviewers use it to check whether you can reason about the pixel pipeline, not just remember a rule.

questions.q: What does `will-change: transform` do, and when is it harmful?
choices: It animates `transform` automatically; harmful if the element has no transition
It hints a layer should be created ahead of time; harmful when overused
It disables layout for the element; harmful if its size ever needs to change
It makes `transform` changes synchronous; harmful on low-end mobile devices
questions.why: `will-change` tells the browser to prepare for a change, typically by promoting the element to its own compositor layer. Each layer costs GPU memory, so applying it to many elements or leaving it on permanently can slow things down. It triggers nothing by itself and does not disable layout.
questions.asked: A deeper rendering question; strong answers mention adding it just before an animation and removing it afterwards.

questions.q: What is `requestAnimationFrame` for in visual updates?
choices: Running a callback on a worker thread so it never blocks the main thread
Running a callback after every task, so the UI updates as soon as possible
Running a callback when the browser is idle and has nothing else to do
Running a callback just before the next frame's style, layout and paint
questions.why: rAF callbacks run once per frame right before rendering, so DOM writes made there are batched into that frame and visual updates line up with the display refresh. It runs on the main thread; idle work is `requestIdleCallback`, and rAF is paused in background tabs.
questions.asked: A foundation for questions about animation jank and scheduling work in the browser.

questions.q: A CSV import parses a 30 MB file in the browser and the page freezes for 4 s. What is the best fix?
choices: Move parsing into a Web Worker and post the results back to the page
Wrap the parsing in `async`/`await` so it runs concurrently with the UI
Parse the file inside `requestAnimationFrame` so it matches the frame rate
Use `setTimeout(parse, 0)` so the parsing runs after the click has finished
questions.why: A worker runs on a separate thread, so the main thread stays free to handle input and paint. Marking a function `async` does not move CPU work off the main thread, and `setTimeout(0)` only delays the same 4-second block; rAF would block a frame instead.
questions.asked: Separates people who know `async` is not parallelism from those who don't.

questions.q: What does this Node 24 snippet print, and what does it show about long tasks?
choices: `timer` then `loop done`: a 0 ms timer interrupts the running loop
`loop done` then `timer`: a timer waits until the current task finishes
`loop done` only: a timer is silently dropped once it is overdue by 200 ms
`timer` and `loop done` together, as the timer runs on another thread
questions.why: JavaScript is single-threaded per event loop: the timer callback is queued but cannot run until the synchronous loop returns, so it fires about 200 ms late. In a browser, a click handler would be delayed the same way, which is the input delay part of INP.
questions.asked: The event-loop basis of every responsiveness question; interviewers expect you to link it to input delay.

questions.q: What does Total Blocking Time (TBT) in a Lighthouse report measure?
choices: The total duration of every task on the main thread during page load
The time from navigation until the page responds to its first input
The sum of each long task's time over 50 ms between FCP and interactive
The time the HTML parser spent blocked on render-blocking scripts alone, in total
questions.why: TBT adds up the part of each task beyond 50 ms between First Contentful Paint and Time to Interactive, so a 120 ms task contributes 70 ms. It is a lab proxy for INP, which Lighthouse cannot measure without real interactions.
questions.asked: Interviewers ask it to check you know TBT is the lab stand-in for INP, not a Core Web Vital itself.

questions.q: What does `Cache-Control: no-cache` mean on an HTML response?
choices: The browser must not store the response anywhere, not even in memory
The browser may store it but must revalidate it before each reuse
The browser may use it for up to one minute, then must drop it
Only CDNs may cache the response; browsers must always refetch
questions.why: `no-cache` allows storage but requires revalidation with the server (for example via `ETag` and `If-None-Match`) every time; a `304 Not Modified` then costs a round trip but no body. Forbidding storage entirely is `no-store`. The names are famously misleading.
questions.asked: Almost everyone confuses `no-cache` and `no-store`; getting it right signals real HTTP experience.

questions.q: An API response is served with `Cache-Control: max-age=60, stale-while-revalidate=300`. What happens on a request 2 minutes after it was cached?
choices: The browser blocks until it has fetched a fresh copy from the server
The browser returns an error because the cached copy has fully expired
The stale copy is used at once and refreshed in the background
The stale copy is used for five more minutes with no network request
questions.why: After `max-age` (60 s) the response is stale, but within the extra 300 s window the cache may serve it immediately while revalidating asynchronously, so the user never waits. The next request gets the refreshed copy. After 360 s it must revalidate before use.
questions.asked: SWR is a common CDN and browser pattern; interviewers want the timeline explained, not just the name.

questions.q: Why do content hashes in asset filenames (such as `app.3f9a1c.js`) matter for cache busting?
choices: Browsers compare the hash with the file's bytes and refuse tampered files
A changed file gets a new URL, so long-cached old copies are never reused
The hash tells the CDN to purge the previous version of the file at once
The hash lets the server compress the file once and reuse the result
questions.why: Caches key on URL, so when content changes the hash (and therefore the URL) changes, and the HTML simply references the new file; old copies can stay cached for a year without harm. Integrity checking is the separate `integrity` (SRI) attribute, and nothing is purged.
questions.asked: Explains why the long `immutable` cache is safe; interviewers pair it with the HTML caching question.

questions.q: What main problem does HTTP/2 multiplexing solve compared with HTTP/1.1?
choices: It encrypts requests, which HTTP/1.1 had no standard way to do
It compresses response bodies, which HTTP/1.1 could not compress
It lets the server push every asset before the browser has asked for it
It runs many requests over one connection without head-of-line waits
questions.why: HTTP/1.1 allows one in-flight request per connection, so browsers opened about six per origin and requests queued behind each other. HTTP/2 interleaves many streams on one connection. HTTP/1.1 already supported gzip and TLS, and server push has been removed from Chrome.
questions.asked: Sets up the follow-up on why old tricks like domain sharding and sprite sheets matter less today.

questions.q: Which advantage does HTTP/3 over QUIC give on a lossy mobile network compared with HTTP/2 over TCP?
choices: A lost packet stalls only its own stream, not every stream on the connection
Responses are smaller, because QUIC compresses bodies better than brotli
It removes the need for TLS, so connections are set up with no handshake at all
It allows browsers to open unlimited connections to the same origin at once
questions.why: TCP delivers bytes in order, so one lost packet blocks every HTTP/2 stream until it is retransmitted (transport-level head-of-line blocking). QUIC runs over UDP with per-stream ordering. QUIC has TLS 1.3 built in and combines the handshakes, but encryption is still mandatory.
questions.asked: A deeper networking question; strong candidates also mention connection migration when a phone changes network.

questions.q: A third-party chat widget adds 600 KB of JavaScript, but most visitors never open it. What is the standard pattern?
choices: Load it with `async` at the top of the `<head>` so it starts downloading first
Load it in a Web Worker so its DOM changes happen off the main thread
Show a lightweight facade and load the real widget on the first interaction
Self-host a copy of the script and give it a one-year `max-age` cache header
questions.why: A facade is a static button that looks like the widget; the real script loads only when the user clicks or hovers, so most visitors pay nothing. `async` still downloads and runs it on every page, workers cannot touch the DOM, and self-hosting a vendor script breaks their updates.
questions.asked: Lighthouse suggests facades for chat and video embeds; interviewers like a concrete example such as a YouTube embed.

questions.q: Why are Core Web Vitals judged at the 75th percentile rather than the average?
choices: The average is dominated by bots, which the 75th percentile filters out
It reflects what most users get while not being skewed by a few outliers
Google only stores the slowest quarter of visits, so p75 is all that exists
The 75th percentile is always lower than the mean, so pages pass more often
questions.why: A percentile says "three in four visits were at least this good", which covers most users including slower devices, while ignoring the extreme tail. Averages hide a bimodal distribution and are pulled around by outliers; p75 is not guaranteed to be lower than the mean.
questions.asked: Interviewers want to hear that you think in distributions, not averages, when reading performance data.

questions.q: You use the `web-vitals` library to collect field data. Why send the metric with `navigator.sendBeacon` rather than `fetch` in a `then`?
questions.code: onINP((m) => navigator.sendBeacon('/rum', JSON.stringify(m)));
choices: `sendBeacon` is the only API the `web-vitals` callbacks are allowed to call
`sendBeacon` compresses the body with brotli, which `fetch` cannot do
INP is often reported as the page is hidden, and a beacon survives unload
`sendBeacon` waits for a response, so you know the metric was stored
questions.why: INP and CLS are only final when the page is hidden or unloaded, which is when the library fires the callback; a normal request may be cancelled then, while a beacon is queued by the browser and sent anyway. `fetch` with `keepalive: true` is the equivalent; a beacon gives you no response at all.
questions.asked: A practical RUM detail; interviewers like candidates who know why field data goes missing.

questions.q: What does `buffered: true` do in this PerformanceObserver call?
choices: It batches entries and delivers them once, when the page is unloaded
It also delivers entries recorded before the observer was registered
It stores entries in `localStorage` so they survive a page reload
It delays the callback until the main thread is idle after `load`
questions.why: Your analytics script usually loads after the LCP candidate has already been painted; `buffered: true` replays entries the browser buffered before `observe` was called. Without it you would miss early entries. It does not persist anything or change when the callback runs.
questions.asked: Shows you have written or debugged RUM code, not just read a dashboard.

questions.q: What does a `Server-Timing` response header give you?
questions.code: Server-Timing: db;dur=182, render;dur=41, cache;desc="miss"
choices: It tells the browser how long to cache the response for each named server layer
It makes the server cancel the request if a stage exceeds its duration
It sets a timeout the browser should apply when it retries the request
It exposes server-side timings in DevTools and to RUM scripts in the page
questions.why: The metrics appear in the DevTools Network panel's Timing tab and in `PerformanceResourceTiming.serverTiming`, so a slow TTFB can be split into database, rendering and cache time from real users. It is purely informational; it controls neither caching nor timeouts.
questions.asked: Connects front-end metrics to back-end causes, which interviewers value in full-stack candidates.

questions.q: Your RUM script reads Resource Timing for images on `cdn.example.com`, but `transferSize` and most phases are 0. Why?
choices: The CDN must send `Timing-Allow-Origin` to expose cross-origin detail
Resource Timing only records resources loaded from the page's own origin
The images came from the memory cache, which is never recorded
Resource Timing only works for scripts and stylesheets, not images
questions.why: Cross-origin resources are recorded, but sizes and detailed phases are zeroed unless the response opts in with `Timing-Allow-Origin`. Images are recorded like any other resource type. A zero `transferSize` can also mean a cache hit, but that would not zero the other phases for same-origin files.
questions.asked: An edge case that trips up teams building their own RUM; knowing it shows hands-on experience.

questions.q: Lighthouse scores for the same page vary between 72 and 88 across runs. What is the sound response?
choices: Take the single best run, since it shows what the page is capable of
Run it several times, use the median, and control the test machine
Switch from mobile to desktop mode, which has no throttling and no variance
Ignore Lighthouse entirely, since lab data cannot be used to find regressions
questions.why: Lab runs vary with CPU load, network and third-party responses; the median of several runs on a consistent machine is the recommended way to compare. Desktop mode still varies, and lab data remains useful for catching regressions in CI as long as you allow for noise.
questions.asked: Tests whether you treat a single Lighthouse number as truth; the right answer mentions medians and field data.

questions.q: Why can PageSpeed Insights show field data for a popular site but "no data" for a new internal admin app?
choices: It comes from CrUX, which needs enough opted-in Chrome users of public pages
Field data is only collected for sites that add Google Analytics to every page
Field data is available only once the site has passed a Lighthouse audit
Field data comes from Search Console, which ignores apps that use a SPA router
questions.why: CrUX aggregates real Chrome users who have opted in, over a rolling 28 days, and only for publicly discoverable origins with enough traffic. Logged-in internal tools rarely qualify, so they need their own RUM. It has nothing to do with Google Analytics or Lighthouse results.
questions.asked: Interviewers want to hear what you would do instead: collect RUM with `web-vitals` and send it to your own backend.

questions.q: You fix a CLS bug and deploy it today. When will PageSpeed Insights' field data fully reflect the fix?
choices: Immediately, because PageSpeed Insights re-runs the page on every request
After the next Lighthouse run in CI updates the Chrome UX Report dataset
After roughly 28 days, as CrUX reports a rolling 28-day window of visits
After Google re-crawls the page, which usually happens within an hour
questions.why: CrUX field data is a rolling 28-day aggregate, so old visits leave the window gradually and a fix shows fully about four weeks later. The lab section updates immediately, but it is a separate simulated run. Your own RUM shows the change the same day.
questions.asked: A practical expectation-setting question; strong answers say you would verify with your own RUM first.

questions.q: What does `performance.measure` add over logging `Date.now()` differences?
choices: It runs the measured code on a background thread so the timing is exact
It sends the measurement to CrUX so it appears in PageSpeed Insights
It pauses the garbage collector, so the measurement excludes GC pauses
It uses a high-resolution clock and shows up in the DevTools timeline
questions.why: User Timing marks and measures use `performance.now()`'s monotonic high-resolution clock and appear in the Performance panel's Timings track, so you can see your code's phases alongside tasks and paints; a RUM script can also read them. They do not affect how code runs or report to CrUX.
questions.asked: Shows you instrument your own code instead of guessing where time goes.

questions.q: What does this Node 24 snippet print?
choices: 600, because the two timers still run one after the other
300, because both timers were started before either finished
0, because `Promise.all` resolves as soon as its array is created
900, because `Promise.all` adds a timer tick for each promise
questions.why: Both promises are created (and their timers started) immediately, then `Promise.all` waits for the slower one, so the total is about 300 ms. Awaiting each in turn would take about 600 ms. That is the same reason independent API calls on page load should be started together.
questions.asked: The request-waterfall question in disguise; interviewers expect the link to data fetching on page load.

questions.q: A page's component tree fetches the user, then the user's team, then the team's projects, each in a child's effect. What is the core performance problem?
choices: A request waterfall: each fetch waits for the previous render and response
React batches the three fetches into one request, which the server rejects
The browser limits a page to one in-flight request per component
Effects run on the server first, so every request is made twice
questions.why: Fetching in child effects means each request starts only after its parent has rendered with the previous response, so latency adds up. Fix it by fetching in parallel at the route level, adding an API that returns what the page needs, or using a router/data library that loads ahead of rendering.
questions.asked: One of the most common real SPA slowdowns; interviewers want a concrete fix, not only the diagnosis.

questions.q: An orders endpoint returns every order (about 40,000 rows, 18 MB of JSON) and the table filters on the client. What is the main fix?
choices: Enable brotli so the 18 MB compresses, which removes the parse cost too
Cache the whole response in `localStorage` so it downloads only once
Paginate and filter on the server so the client receives one page
Switch from JSON to XML, which browsers parse faster on the main thread
questions.why: Server-side pagination and filtering bound the payload, the database work and the client's parse and render time. Compression shrinks the transfer but the browser still parses 18 MB; `localStorage` is small, synchronous and goes stale; XML is not faster to parse.
questions.asked: Every CRUD interview touches on pagination; tying it to performance on both ends is a strong signal.

questions.q: What does `Cache-Control: public, max-age=0, s-maxage=300` tell caches?
choices: Browsers may cache it for 300 s and shared caches must always revalidate
Browsers and CDNs may both cache it for 300 s, and it is then discarded
It is only cached when the request contains no cookies or auth headers
Browsers must revalidate each time; shared caches may keep it for 300 s
questions.why: `s-maxage` applies only to shared caches and overrides `max-age` there, so a CDN can serve the page for five minutes while browsers revalidate. That lets you absorb traffic at the edge and still purge or roll out changes quickly. Cookies alone do not change these directives.
questions.asked: Separating browser and CDN lifetimes is a standard caching design question.

questions.q: An API returns per-user data. Which header stops a CDN from serving one user's response to another?
choices: `Cache-Control: private, max-age=60`
`Cache-Control: public, max-age=60`
`Cache-Control: immutable, max-age=60`
`Cache-Control: s-maxage=60, public`
questions.why: `private` allows only the user's own browser cache to store it, so shared caches must not. `public` and `s-maxage` explicitly permit shared caching, and `immutable` only says the body will not change during its lifetime. For sensitive data, `no-store` is safer still.
questions.asked: Caching personal data at the edge is a real incident class; interviewers check you know the guard.

questions.q: Your server varies the body by `Accept-Encoding` (brotli or gzip). Which header must the response include so a CDN caches it correctly?
choices: `Content-Encoding: identity`
`Vary: Accept-Encoding`
`Accept-Ranges: bytes`
`Transfer-Encoding: chunked`
questions.why: `Vary` tells caches which request headers were used to choose the response, so they keep a brotli and a gzip copy and serve each to matching clients. Without it a cache might hand brotli bytes to a client that cannot decode them. The other headers describe the body or transfer, not cache keys.
questions.asked: A subtle caching bug; strong candidates also warn against `Vary: User-Agent` fragmenting the cache.

questions.q: Why do builds often pre-compress static assets with brotli at level 11 instead of compressing on each request?
choices: Level 11 is the only brotli level that all browsers are able to decode
Pre-compressed files are served with no `Content-Encoding` header
Level 11 is too slow per request, but at build time it costs nothing
On-the-fly compression breaks the file's content hash in its URL
questions.why: Brotli's highest levels give the smallest files but are far too slow to run per request; static files can be compressed once at build time and served as `.br`. Dynamic responses use a fast level (around 4–5). Browsers decode every level, and the header is still sent.
questions.asked: Shows you know compression is a CPU-versus-bytes trade-off that differs for static and dynamic responses.

questions.q: What should an image already in JPEG or WebP format get from the server's compression settings?
choices: Nothing: it is already compressed, so gzip or brotli gains little
Brotli at level 11, which usually halves the size of photographic images
Gzip, since browsers cannot decode brotli on binary responses
Gzip and then brotli applied in turn, for the smallest possible file
questions.why: JPEG, WebP, AVIF, WOFF2 and video are already compressed, so a generic compressor saves almost nothing and wastes CPU. Text formats (HTML, CSS, JS, JSON, SVG) are what brotli and gzip are for. Browsers decode brotli for any content type.
questions.asked: A quick check that you know where compression pays off.

questions.q: How does an image CDN typically serve AVIF only to browsers that support it, from a single URL?
choices: It sniffs the `User-Agent` and hard-codes a list of supporting browsers
