It sends AVIF to everyone, relying on browsers to convert it to JPEG
It reads the `Accept` header and responds with `Vary: Accept`
It serves AVIF only over HTTP/3, which every AVIF browser supports
questions.why: Browsers list the image formats they accept in the request's `Accept` header, so the CDN can negotiate the format and must send `Vary: Accept` so caches keep one copy per format. User-agent lists go stale, browsers do not transcode, and format support is unrelated to protocol.
questions.asked: Contrasts server-side negotiation with `<picture>`; strong answers mention the cache-key implication.

questions.q: What is the main trade-off of AVIF compared with WebP for photos?
choices: AVIF has no alpha channel, so it cannot replace PNG with transparency
AVIF files are usually smaller, but encoding is slower and costlier
AVIF decodes on the GPU only, so it is not shown on older phones
AVIF files are larger, but they always decode faster than WebP
questions.why: AVIF usually beats WebP on size at the same visual quality, but it is much slower to encode, which matters for on-the-fly image services, and can be slower to decode. It supports transparency and HDR, and baseline browser support is now broad.
questions.asked: Interviewers want a format choice justified with trade-offs, not a blanket "always use AVIF".

questions.q: An ad slot loads after the article text and pushes it down. Which fix addresses the CLS?
choices: Load the ad script with `defer` instead of `async` so it runs later
Give the slot `display: none` until the ad arrives, then show it
Put the ad inside an `<iframe>`, which never contributes to layout shift
Reserve the slot's space with `min-height` for the likely ad size
questions.why: Reserving space means the ad fills an existing box instead of creating one, so nothing moves. Changing when the script runs or toggling `display` still inserts a box after content has painted, and an iframe that grows shifts content just like any other element.
questions.asked: A standard CLS fix; strong answers mention choosing the most common size, or showing a placeholder when no ad fills.

questions.q: What does the CSS `aspect-ratio` property help with in a card grid of embedded videos?
questions.code: .embed { width: 100%; aspect-ratio: 16 / 9; }
choices: It crops the video to 16:9 so the player downloads fewer pixels
It sizes the box from its width, reserving space before the iframe loads
It tells the browser to pick a 16:9 video rendition from the server
It stops the browser from painting the embed until it has fully loaded
questions.why: With a width and `aspect-ratio`, the browser can calculate the height immediately, so the iframe loads into a correctly sized box and no content shifts. It does not crop media, choose renditions or delay painting; it replaces the old padding-top percentage hack.
questions.asked: Checks you know the modern CSS tool for reserving space for things that are not `` tags.

questions.q: A search box calls the API on every keystroke. Which technique cuts the requests without making typing feel slower?
choices: Throttle to one request per second, sending the first keystroke only
Disable the input while each request is in flight to avoid overlap
Debounce so a request fires only after a short pause in typing
Cache every response in `sessionStorage` before sending the request
questions.why: Debouncing (typically 200–300 ms) waits until the user pauses, so "laptop" costs one request rather than six, and cancelling stale requests avoids out-of-order results. Throttling sends intermediate queries and may drop the final one if not set up carefully; disabling the input blocks typing.
questions.asked: Interviewers often follow up with "and how do you stop an earlier slow response overwriting a later one?".

questions.q: Why use `IntersectionObserver` instead of a `scroll` listener that calls `getBoundingClientRect()` to trigger infinite scrolling?
choices: It is the only way to detect scrolling inside an element with `overflow: auto`
It runs in a Web Worker, so none of its callbacks use the main thread
It fetches the next page by itself when the sentinel element is visible
The browser computes visibility itself, so there is no layout work per scroll
questions.why: A scroll handler runs many times per second and each `getBoundingClientRect()` can force layout; `IntersectionObserver` lets the browser track intersections off that hot path and calls you only when visibility changes. The callback still runs on the main thread and you still write the fetch yourself.
questions.asked: A common implementation question for lazy loading and infinite lists.

questions.q: What does `{ passive: true }` on a `touchstart` or `wheel` listener promise the browser?
choices: That it will not call `preventDefault()`, so scrolling need not wait for it
That the handler runs only once and is then removed automatically
That the handler may run on a background thread, well off the main thread
That the handler will fire only after the scroll gesture has finished
questions.why: Scrolling on touch and wheel normally has to wait for listeners in case they cancel it; a passive listener promises not to, so the compositor scrolls immediately. `once: true` is the auto-remove option, and handlers always run on the main thread.
questions.asked: Lighthouse flags non-passive listeners; interviewers want to know you understand why.

questions.q: What does a Service Worker's stale-while-revalidate strategy do for a request?
choices: It always goes to the network first and uses the cache only when offline
It serves the cached copy at once and updates the cache from the network
It serves only from the cache and never contacts the network again
It races the cache and network and discards whichever loses
questions.why: The response comes from the cache immediately while a network request refreshes the cache for next time, so users get speed at the cost of seeing a one-visit-old copy. Network-first uses the cache only as a fallback; cache-only never updates.
questions.asked: Interviewers ask you to pick a strategy per resource type, for example cache-first for hashed assets and network-first for HTML.

questions.q: Why does server-side rendering usually improve LCP but can hurt INP on a React page?
choices: SSR skips hydration, so event handlers are attached only on first click
SSR sends HTML only after all data loads, which delays every interaction
SSR moves all rendering to the server, so the client can no longer update
HTML shows early, but hydration is a long task during which clicks wait
questions.why: The server's HTML lets content paint without waiting for JavaScript, but the client still has to download the bundle and hydrate, and interactions during that long task are delayed. Streaming, selective hydration and shipping less JavaScript (such as Server Components) reduce the cost.
questions.asked: Tests whether you see rendering strategies as metric trade-offs rather than a free win.

questions.q: A Node 24 API server shows TTFB of 2 s for the product page, but the CPU is idle. Which is the most likely cause to check first?
choices: Sequential database or HTTP calls, each awaited one after the other
The HTML is too large, so the first byte waits for gzip to finish first
Node's event loop cannot run more than one request at a time
The response is missing `Cache-Control`, so the browser keeps refetching
questions.why: An idle CPU with a slow response means the server is waiting on I/O; the common cause is awaiting independent queries in series, or an N+1 pattern. Measure with tracing or `Server-Timing`, then parallelise, batch or cache. Node handles many concurrent requests while awaiting I/O.
questions.asked: A full-stack question that checks you can move from a front-end metric to a back-end cause.

questions.q: Which is a sensible bundle budget to enforce in CI for a React SPA's initial route?
choices: A limit on the total size of `node_modules` on the build machine
A limit on the number of npm packages listed in package.json
A limit on the compressed JavaScript loaded for the first route
A limit on the uncompressed size of the source files in `src/`
questions.why: What users pay for is the JavaScript the first route actually downloads and parses, so budgets are set per entry or route, usually on the compressed (and sometimes parsed) size, with tools like size-limit. Dependency counts and source size correlate poorly with what ships.
questions.asked: Interviewers want to hear what you would measure and where in the pipeline it would fail the build.

questions.q: A PR's size check fails: the initial chunk grew by 90 KB after adding a date picker used only on the settings page. What is the best fix?
choices: Raise the budget by 90 KB, since the date picker is a legitimate feature
Lazy-load the settings route or the picker so it leaves the initial chunk
Minify the picker twice, which removes the extra whitespace that it adds
Move the picker to `devDependencies` so the bundler skips it
questions.why: The code is needed only on one page, so a dynamic import moves it into a chunk loaded when that page opens and the initial route stays within budget. Raising the budget hides the regression; minifiers are idempotent; `devDependencies` does not affect what imported code the bundler includes.
questions.asked: Shows you treat a budget failure as a design prompt rather than an obstacle.

questions.q: What is a vendor chunk, and why can splitting it out help repeat visits?
choices: A chunk for third-party ads, so they load from the vendor's own CDN
A chunk that is inlined into the HTML so it never needs a separate request
A chunk built without minification so vendors can debug their code
Rarely changing libraries in their own hashed file, cached across deploys
questions.why: When libraries like React are in a separate chunk, deploying a change to your app code changes only the app chunk's hash, so returning users re-download just that. Too many tiny chunks add requests and hurt compression, so bundlers group by change frequency.
questions.asked: Links bundling to caching; interviewers like the point that fewer bytes on repeat visits is the real goal.

questions.q: Which tool gives you a treemap of what is inside your production bundle?
choices: `rollup-plugin-visualizer` for Vite, or `source-map-explorer` on the output
`npm ls --all`, which lists every installed package along with its version
`tsc --listFiles`, which prints each file that the TypeScript compiler reads
`npm audit`, which lists every dependency the build pulls in
questions.why: Visualisers read the bundle (or its source maps) and show how many bytes each module contributes after tree shaking and minification. `npm ls` lists installed packages, not what ships; `tsc --listFiles` shows type-checking inputs; `npm audit` reports vulnerabilities.
questions.asked: The first step of any bundle-size investigation; interviewers want to know you measure before you change.

questions.q: A detached DOM node keeps growing in a heap snapshot after each modal open and close. What usually causes it?
choices: The modal uses CSS animations, which keep every frame in memory
The browser caches closed modals in the bfcache for later reuse
A listener or variable still references the removed modal's elements
React keeps a copy of each unmounted tree so that DevTools can inspect it
questions.why: Removed elements stay in memory while anything reachable references them: a `window` listener not removed on close, a module-level array or a closure in a timer. Clean up in the effect's return function or with an `AbortController`. The bfcache stores whole pages, not elements.
questions.asked: Memory leaks in long-lived SPAs are a real support issue; interviewers look for the cleanup habit.

questions.q: What does `contain: layout` on a widget tell the browser?
choices: The widget is hidden until it is scrolled into view, then laid out
Layout inside the widget does not affect anything outside it
The widget's layout is computed on the GPU instead of the CPU
The widget may not be larger than its parent's content box
questions.why: Layout containment lets the browser limit relayout to the widget's subtree when something inside it changes, which helps on large pages with frequently updating components. Skipping off-screen rendering is `content-visibility: auto`, and layout never moves to the GPU.
questions.asked: A deeper rendering question; strong answers relate it to `content-visibility` and when each applies.

questions.q: Why do inline SVG icons repeated 200 times in a table cost more than using `<use>` with a sprite?
choices: Inline SVG is always rasterised on the CPU, while sprites use the GPU
Inline SVG cannot be cached, whereas `<use>` references are cached by URL
Each inline copy duplicates the path data in the HTML and the DOM
Browsers download a separate file for each inline SVG in the page
questions.why: Every inline copy adds its full path data to the HTML payload and to the DOM, which grows parse, style and memory costs; a `<symbol>` referenced by `<use>` defines it once. Inline SVG needs no extra request and both forms are painted the same way.
questions.asked: Relevant to icon-heavy CRUD tables; interviewers like candidates who notice DOM size as a cost.

questions.q: Which is the better first step when a stakeholder says "the app feels slow"?
choices: Upgrade the framework to its latest major version, which is usually faster
Rewrite the slowest-looking component with `useMemo` and `useCallback`
Add a CDN in front of everything, since network is almost always the cause
Find which page and interaction is slow, and measure it with field data
questions.why: "Slow" could mean slow load (LCP), laggy clicks (INP), jumping content (CLS) or a slow API; each has a different fix. Identify the page and metric from RUM or a reproduction, profile it, then change one thing and re-measure. Upgrading or memoising blindly rarely fixes the real bottleneck.
questions.asked: An open-ended question where the method matters more than any specific technique.
